processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Five different alloys were synthesized in one operation using five movable Cu molds successively filled with melt from a 4-kg ingot; after each cast the remaining melt composition was adjusted by charging Al through an air lock.
10×50×130 mm³ cast blocks were hot rolled into 2±0.1 mm thick and ~500 mm long sheets.
After water quenching, the sheets were cut perpendicular to the rolling direction into sets of nine segments with dimensions 2×60×55 mm³ for each alloy composition.
This aging step (600 °C, 1 h) defines the sample condition. After the heat treatments, scales were removed from the surfaces by low-pressure, fine-grit sandblasting.

structures.overall_structure: Fully recrystallized microstructure (after hot rolling and water quenching) with grain size ~20 μm and some retained Mn microsegregations. For the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl alloy class, XRD screening shows increasing ferrite content with Al (2–11 wt.%), which dominates the property trend over κ-carbides or ε-martensite.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: tensile specimens prepared from the segments by package spark erosion
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: All plotted values represent averages of three measurements for every material state.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: performed on the rolling plane of samples ground to a thickness of 1 mm
characterization_methods.purpose: phase characterization / screening of constituting phases
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl class, increasing ferrite content with Al (2–11 wt.%) is more relevant for the mechanical trend than κ-carbides or ε-martensite.

unmapped_findings: For the Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl alloy family, the paper reports only a class-level trend: yield strength and ultimate tensile strength both increase while tensile elongation drops as Al content increases over 2–11 wt.%; XRD screening indicates increasing ferrite content is more relevant to this trend than κ-carbides or ε-martensite (block b0026). No sample-specific YS/UTS/TE/hardness values are reported for the 600 °C/1 h aging condition.

Figure 6 mechanical-property plots for Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl show only the as-quenched, 400 °C/24 h, 500 °C/24 h and 600 °C/24 h conditions; the 600 °C/1 h condition (this sample) is not plotted, so its individual strength/elongation/hardness values are not available in this paper.

For austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels generally, κ-carbides have an ordered fcc L′1₂ structure with approximate stoichiometry (Fe,Mn)₃AlC and a lattice mismatch below 3% with respect to an austenitic Fe-Mn-C matrix (block b0015); these statements are not tied to the specific 600 °C/1 h Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl sample.

This sample belongs to a 45-condition RAP matrix (five alloys × nine heat treatments per base composition); the individual Al levels of the five Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl alloys within the 2–11 wt.% range are not enumerated in the paper (blocks b0019, b0020, b0109).

The paper presents a temperature-sensitive constitutive strain-hardening model for low-SFE fcc/TWIP steels and discusses κ-carbide Orowan-loop contributions (blocks b0036–b0100), but the model is not applied to specific Fe-20Mn-0.4C-xAl 600 °C/1 h data in this paper.
